questions.question: For a series of functions $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$, what are its partial sums?
When do we say that $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$ converges to $f$ on $X$?
options: When the partial sums $S_N$ converge to $f$ pointwise or uniformly on $X$.
When each single term $f_n(x)$ converges to $f(x)$ as $n\to\infty$, for each point $x\in X$.
When the terms satisfy $f_n(x)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, for every $x\in X$.
When the partial sums $S_N$ are uniformly bounded on $X$, for all $N$.

questions.question: Let $f_n(x) = x^n$ and define $S_N(x) = \sum_{n = 1}^{N} f_n(x)$. What is $S_3(x)$?
If $f_n(x) = \dfrac{x}{2^n}$, what is the second partial sum $S_2(x)$?
How is an infinite sum of functions defined?
options: It is always defined by multiplying all functions together.
It is defined only at a single point of $X$.
It ignores the behaviour of finite partial sums.
It is the limit of its partial sums, when they converge.

questions.question: For Riemann-integrable terms on $X=[a,b]$ with finite $a<b$, which convergence hypothesis is used by the stated integration theorem?
options: The series $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$ converges pointwise on $X$.
The terms $f_n$ themselves converge uniformly to $0$ on $X$.
The series $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n'$ of derivatives converges uniformly on $X$.
The series $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$ converges uniformly on $X$.

questions.question: Let $X=[a,b]$ with finite $a<b$. Suppose $f_n$ are Riemann integrable and $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$ converges uniformly on $X$. Which term-by-term integration formula is valid?
Assume the stated differentiability result applies. If $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n \to f$ and $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n' \rightrightarrows g$ on $(a,b)$, what is $f'$ on $(a,b)$?
Why is it not enough to look only at the individual functions $f_n$ when defining $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$?
options: Because convergence is a statement about the sequence of partial sums $S_N$.
Because each $f_n$ must be integrated first, and the series is the sum of those integrals.
Because the individual $f_n$ need not be defined at every point of $X$.
Because convergence requires the partial sums to be increasing in $N$.

questions.question: Which series of functions fails to converge at some point of $(-1,1)$?
On a finite closed interval $X=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, a student invokes the stated uniform-convergence theorem to integrate Riemann-integrable terms. Which hypothesis must they check?
options: The existence of the very first partial sum $S_1$ only.
The fact that $X$ has at least one point.

questions.question: Let $S_N(x) = \sum_{n = 1}^{N} f_n(x)$ and suppose $S_N$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $X$. Which conclusion matches the definition?
options: $f_N$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $X$ by definition of the series.
$\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n$ cannot be assigned a function limit.

questions.question: How is an infinite series of functions defined through partial sums?
options: By studying the limit of the individual terms $f_N(x)$ as $N\to\infty$.
By studying the limit of $\prod_{n=1}^N f_n(x)$ as $N\to\infty$.
By studying the limit of $S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)$ as $N\to\infty$.
By studying the limit of the averages $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)$ as $N\to\infty$.

questions.question: Why is uniform convergence stronger than pointwise convergence for a series of functions?
options: Each point may use an unrelated bound with no common control.
Only the first term is checked.
The same tail bound must work for all points in the domain.
The functions must all be constant.

questions.question: What does the notation $f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n(x)$ mean?
options: The partial sums converge to the function $f$ at the relevant points.
The individual terms $f_n(x)$ converge to $f(x)$ at the relevant points.
The partial sums $S_N(x)$ equal $f(x)$ exactly, for all large enough $N$.
The series converges uniformly to $f$ on the whole of $X$.

questions.question: If $f_n(x)=n x$, what is $S_3(x)=\sum_{n=1}^3 f_n(x)$?
If $f_n(x)=\frac{1}{2^n}$, what is $S_2(x)$?
The series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!}$ has which convergence property on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: It converges pointwise on $\mathbb{R}$ and uniformly on every compact interval.
It is not a series of functions on $\mathbb{R}$ because its individual terms contain different powers of the variable $x$.

questions.question: On a finite closed interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, which condition is sufficient for term-by-term integration?
options: Pointwise convergence of the series together with Riemann integrability of the terms.
Uniform convergence of the terms $f_n$ to $0$ together with their Riemann integrability.
Uniform convergence of the series together with Riemann integrability of the terms.
Absolute convergence of $\sum f_n(x)$ at every point, with each $f_n$ continuous.

questions.question: Let $X=[a,b]$ with finite $a<b$. If $f_n$ are Riemann integrable and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n$ converges uniformly on $X$, which formula is supported?
